posts.post_subject: Newbee wants to start and found optics / mirror / book...
posts.content_md:
The easiest way to start would be to get the Integraf kit (link at top of page). The kit contains everything you need, except for a stable table. For this, you need something pretty heavy that will isolate the components from ground vibrations. You can use a slab of stone (marble, cement etc). Some people on this forum use doors, metal slabs. Anything solid and heavy.

The best books to buy are Graham Saxby's "Practical Holography", reviewed by two of our forum members, Colin ( [http://www.designerinlight.com/holo/graham.htm](http://www.designerinlight.com/holo/graham.htm) ) and Michael ( [http://www.dragonseye.com/holography/re ... axby3.html](http://www.dragonseye.com/holography/reviews_saxby3.html) ), and Fred Untersehers "Holography Handbook" ( [http://www.rossbooks.com/HH/hh.html](http://www.rossbooks.com/HH/hh.html) ). The handbook contains detailed descriptions on how to make a hologram. I would also suggest buying the beamsplitter. This is because if you continue, you'll need to make an interferometer to test stability and you need a beamsplitter to do this. As you get more experienced and familiar, most members of this forum have access to reasonably priced equipment and can help and/or suggest methods/equipment.

posts.content_md:
The little intergraf trays aren't bad, that way you don't waste much chemistry. I use those disposable gladware trays for my processing now, you can seal the lids when you're done (I only reuse the bleach though). Saxby's book is good, I bought it and it was well worth the money. If you get the kit from Intergraf, it has some documents that come with it that will get you started though.

You don't need a ton of optics to make a good hologram though - in this setup only two first surface mirrors are used to enhance the illumination of the object. The stuff in the lower left corner isn't being used for this hologram.

![Image](http://members.shaw.ca/ted.park/images/holotable1.jpg)

posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** I use three + water. What are you using?

I use two water trays. I put all the trays in a row and work my way down:

Developer -> Water (or Stop) -> Bleach -> Water -> Photoflo

I'm in the process of buying some decent trays now. I'll probably get an extra one or two so I can experiment with 2-step developers and/or maybe a fix step?

BTW- I'm not using a running rinse for two reasons: I don't have a sink in my garage (yet!), and I don't know if it is harmful to use tap water vs. distilled for rinsing? Right now I'm just using distilled for everything.

> **tpark:** The little intergraf trays aren't bad, that way you don't waste much chemistry

That's true. And since they aren't square, you don't get the plate stuck in a corner when processing by hand. I took advantage of their 4"x5" plate special when I bought my kit. I was disappointed that the trays wouldn't fit the plates they gave me! 

-Phil

I've been using distilled water everywhere, as the water we have here is quite hard. I suspect you're right though - I've done post wetting rinsing with tap water, and had good results.

PFG-03M - 800-1600 microjoules/cm**2

Exposure rate: 

JD-4 developer

Develop - 15 seconds, or longer (up to about 30 seconds) if it needs it

rinse1 - 25 seconds

bleach - until clear, then another 10 seconds

rinse2 - 30 seconds

wetting - 40 seconds to 1 minute

rinse3 - 30 seconds

> **tpark:** Colin Kaminski wrote:I have seen good evidence that it is better to use distilled at all rinses before bleach and that it does not matter after the bleach.I've been using distilled water everywhere, as the water we have here is quite hard. I suspect you're right though - I've done post wetting rinsing with tap water, and had good results.

I understand the larger problem is in the chlorine. In my water supply it is in the form of chloramines which are very difficult to filter. My RO, as long as I go slow enough, works well but if I push the speed it lets some through. It is my understanding the only to filter chloramines is to use very slow passes through activated carbon or distillation. Normal chlorine like they used to use here is easily filtered out by carbon filters.
